country.comment: Study examines four cities (Bhopal, Indore, Gwalior, and Jabalpur) in the State of Madhya Pradesh, India.

effect_estimate.comment: Descriptive percentages/counts from PPSA city-wide mapping and uncontrolled post-project outputs from the SESI pilot; no inferential statistical test, confidence interval, or p-value is reported.
effect_estimate.value: PPSA spatial poverty mapping across 4 cities identified 1,537 poverty pockets (475,368 households: Bhopal 380 PPs/128,170 HHs; Indore 604 PPs/176,545 HHs; Gwalior 229 PPs/60,787 HHs; Jabalpur 324 PPs/109,866 HHs), revealing 55%–65% under-reporting of poverty pockets in official records (e.g., 380 PPs with ~640,850 residents vs. 209 slums with 125,720 persons in Bhopal's 2001 Census) and large numbers of non-notified slums excluded from city-wide planning. Across mapped poverty pockets, piped water supply reached 30.8% (Bhopal), 28% (Indore), 65.14% (Gwalior), and 34.3% (Jabalpur) of households; improved water access averaged 95.80%, 66%, 96.11%, and 96%; improved sanitation averaged 58.0%, 84%, 68.49%, and 54%; open defecation was 42%, 16%, 31.50%, and 45.7%; nearly 40% of residents in selected slums had water for <1 hour/day and summer fetching took 4–5 hours/day. Using PPSA prioritization, participatory governance (63 Community Water and Sanitation Committees, SHGs, NGO-municipal partnerships), and revolving sanitation loans across 65 slums under SESI produced reported end-of-project outputs of 60 open-defecation-free slums, 20,000 families with household toilets, 15 community toilets, 20 school sanitation blocks, 50 restored water sources, and 1,000 m of drainage (descriptive results only; no inferential effect estimate, CI, or p-value reported).

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by mixed-methods/descriptive design ceiling (MMAT). Assigned 2 because the study directly observes and documents the administrative/governance mechanisms in field implementation: official municipal/Census under-enumeration and non-notification excluding informal settlements from city-wide planning, and PPSA spatial poverty mapping, MAPP participatory planning, NGO-municipal-corporator coordination, CWASCs/SHGs, and revolving sanitation loan funds targeting water and sanitation investments to vulnerable slums.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Study explicitly combines primary quantitative/spatial physical survey mapping across all poverty pockets in four cities (Table 1; plus household baseline KAP surveys in selected PPs) with separate primary qualitative participatory surveys (6 PPs per city), key informant interviews, and group discussions for triangulation, alongside descriptive post-project output reporting of the SESI pilot without a non-randomized comparator group. MMAT is the matching tool for a mixed-methods empirical study.

study_design.comment: Combines a city-wide Poverty Pocket Situation Analysis (PPSA) physical/GIS mapping survey (derived from key informant interviews, group discussions, locality baseline surveys, and household-level KAP baseline surveys in selected slums) triangulated with participatory qualitative surveys in 6 PPs per city, plus descriptive uncontrolled pilot project evaluation of the Slum Environmental Sanitation Initiative (SESI) implemented from 2005 to 2012.
study_design.value: Mixed-methods situational analysis and descriptive pilot intervention case study (city-wide poverty-pocket physical/GIS baseline mapping survey, key informant interviews, group discussions, participatory qualitative slum surveys, household KAP baseline survey, and uncontrolled post-intervention output reporting)
